summary.text: Genetics studies genes, the differences between them, and how traits are passed down in living things.
Gregor Mendel, a friar in 19th-century Brno, was the first to study it scientifically, tracing traits from parents to offspring in pea plants.
Modern genetics also studies how genes function and behave, and how they work together with an organism's environment and experiences.

items.prompt: Two corn seeds have identical genes. One is planted in a mild, wet climate and one in a dry climate, and the dry one ends up much shorter. What best explains this?

options.label: The dry plant's genes changed to match the dry soil
Genes only work in mild climates, not dry ones
The environment can limit growth even when genes are the same
Identical seeds always grow to the same height

items.explain: Genes set an average height the plant could reach, but a lack of water and nutrients held the dry plant to half the height.

items.prompt: A 19th-century breeder believes offspring always get a smooth mix of their parents' traits. What did Mendel's pea experiments show against this?

options.label: Traits come from distinct genes in combination, not a continuous blend
Offspring always look exactly like one parent
Traits only change when the plant is moved to a new place
Parents pass on only the traits they have strengthened

items.explain: Mendel found traits were not blended after hybridization, which showed they are produced by combinations of distinct genes.

items.prompt: A weightlifter trains for ten years and builds huge muscles. Based on what is now known, how do those years of training affect the genes passed to her children?

options.label: Her strengthened traits are passed on to her children
Her genes shift a little with each year of training
Her genes change, but only in her sons
They do not change; experiences don't affect inherited genes

items.explain: The idea that individuals inherit traits strengthened by their parents is now known to be wrong, because experiences do not affect the genes passed on.

items.prompt: A researcher in the early 1900s examines a mealworm and finds cells with both an X and a Y chromosome. Going by Nettie Stevens's findings, what sex is it?

options.label: Female
Male
Either one
Neither one

items.explain: Stevens discovered that females had only the X chromosome while males had both X and Y.

items.prompt: In 1911 a scientist argued that genes are located on chromosomes. What observation did he build the argument on?

options.label: Seed shapes handed down in pea plants
Differences in height between dry and wet corn
A white eye mutation in fruit flies that was linked to sex
Sex differences in chromosomes of mealworms

items.explain: Thomas Hunt Morgan based his argument on a sex-linked white eye mutation he observed in fruit flies.

items.prompt: A farmer saves seed only from her biggest squash each year, hoping the next crop will be bigger. What observation is she relying on?

options.label: Living things inherit traits from their parents
A plant's size depends only on its water supply
Seeds change to match what the farmer wants
Traits skip generations at random

items.explain: Since prehistoric times, people have used the fact that living things inherit traits from their parents to improve crops through selective breeding.

steps.text: A man trains for years and builds big arms.
His training changes the genes he carries.
He passes those changed genes to his child.
So his child is born with bigger arms.

beats.explain: Experiences of individuals do not affect the genes they pass to their children, so the training leaves the inherited genes unchanged.

paragraphs.heading: What genetics studies
paragraphs.text: Genetics is the study of genes, of genetic variation and of heredity, the patterns by which traits are handed down from parents to offspring. It is an important part of biology because heredity is vital to how organisms evolve. Modern genetics also looks at how genes work and behave, studying them inside the cell, in whole organisms and across populations. It has many branches, among them molecular genetics, epigenetics, population genetics and paleogenetics.

paragraphs.heading: Genes and surroundings
paragraphs.text: Genes do not act alone: they work together with an organism's environment and experiences to shape how it develops and behaves, a pairing often called nature versus nurture. A classic example uses two genetically identical seeds of corn. One is planted where the climate is mild and one where it is dry. Their genes set the average height they could reach, but the plant in the dry place grows only half as tall, because it lacks water and nutrients.

paragraphs.heading: Mendel's peas
paragraphs.text: Gregor Mendel, a friar working in Brno in the 1800s, was the first to study genetics scientifically. Working with pea plants, he traced how certain traits were passed on and described the patterns with mathematics, presenting his paper in 1865. He saw that the plants inherited traits through separate units of inheritance, a term still used for what we call a gene. His work suggested that heredity comes in particles rather than being acquired, and that simple rules and ratios could explain how many traits are inherited.

paragraphs.heading: Ideas Mendel overturned
paragraphs.text: People made use of inheritance long before science explained it, breeding better crops and animals since prehistoric times. In the 1800s a popular idea was blending inheritance, in which offspring get a smooth mix of their parents' traits. Mendel found cases where traits plainly did not blend after crossing, which pointed to distinct genes instead. What looks like blending is now explained by several genes with quantitative effects. Another idea, often linked to Lamarck, held that children inherit traits their parents strengthened, and it is now known to be wrong.

paragraphs.heading: A forerunner
paragraphs.text: Before Mendel, the Hungarian noble Imre Festetics was the first to use the word genetic about heredity, and he is considered the first geneticist. In 1819 he described several rules of inheritance. He concluded from observation that organisms inherit their characteristics rather than acquire them. He also proposed that traits of past generations could reappear later.

paragraphs.heading: Finding genes on chromosomes
paragraphs.text: Mendel's importance was not widely grasped until 1900, by which time he had died; that year Hugo de Vries and other scientists rediscovered his research. William Bateson coined the word genetics in 1905. Scientists then hunted for the molecules in cells that carry inheritance. Nettie Stevens, studying mealworms, found that females had only the X chromosome while males had both X and Y, and concluded that sex depends on chromosomes and is set by the male. In 1911 Thomas Hunt Morgan argued that genes sit on chromosomes, based on a sex-linked white-eye mutation in fruit flies.
